title: Multi-Criteria Evaluation of Cryogenic Holding Time Effects on AA7075-T6 Milling Performance
abstract: Abstract Machining of AA7075-T6 is challenged by high cutting temperature, process instability, and multiple interacting performance responses. This study investigates the effect of deep cryogenic holding time (CHT) on the milling performance of AA7075-T6 through a combined experimental and multi-criteria optimization approach. The material was cryogenically treated at − 146 °C for 12, 24, and 36 h, while untreated specimens were used as the reference condition. Milling experiments were carried out using a full factorial design with cutting speed (200, 250, and 300 m/min), feed per tooth (0.08, 0.10, and 0.12 mm/tooth), and CHT as control factors. Machining performance was evaluated based on the resultant cutting force, vibration, cutting temperature, power consumption, and surface roughness. In addition, microstructural and mechanical changes were examined by X-ray diffraction, SEM/EDS observations, and hardness measurements. The results showed that increasing CHT led to a measurable increase in hardness and induced lattice modifications, which influenced the thermo-mechanical behavior during machining without forming new phases. Among the machining responses, CHT had the strongest effect on cutting temperature and also contributed to a reduction in cutting force, whereas vibration, surface roughness, and power consumption were primarily affected by cutting parameters. Entropy-weighted grey relational analysis identified the optimal condition as 36 h CHT, a cutting speed of 250 m/min, and a feed per tooth of 0.08 mm. Under this condition, cutting force, temperature, and vibration were reduced by 23.7%, 35.0%, and 52.1%, respectively, relative to the reference condition. These findings demonstrate that cryogenic pre-treatment, combined with cutting parameters, can improve milling performance and process stability in AA7075-T6.
journal: International Journal of Precision Engineering and Manufacturing

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Aluminum 7075 (AA7075) is a high-strength alloy widely used in aerospace, defense, and automotive industries due to its high mechanical performance (yield strength ≈ 410–470 MPa, ultimate tensile strength ≈ 485–530 MPa, Tm ≈ 635 °C [ 1 ] and Vickers hardness (HV 0.05) ≈ 160 [ 2 ,  3 ]), ductility, good corrosion resistance, and thermal conductivity capable of rapid heat dissipation [ 4 ,  5 – 6 ]. Despite these advantages, its machining remains challenging, particularly at high speeds, where rapid temperature rise and high strain rates can alter material flow behavior and promote thermomechanical instabilities that adversely affect process stability and surface integrity [ 7 ]. In milling chip formation is governed by severe plastic deformation under high strain rates and elevated temperatures, where the coupled evolution of stress and temperature controls the flow response [ 8 ,  9 ].

Cryogenic treatment has attracted increasing attention as a pre-treatment to improve machinability by modifying the microstructural state and thermo-mechanical response of metallic materials. Typically performed at temperatures near liquid-nitrogen conditions (approximately − 140 to − 196 °C) [ 21 ], this process does not introduce new phases in precipitation-hardened aluminum alloys; instead, thermal contraction mismatch between the matrix and second-phase constituents can generate persistent micro-stress fields within the microstructure [ 22 ]. These micro-stresses cause the reorientation of existing dislocations, particularly at phase interfaces, leading to the development of dislocation clusters and cell-like substructures [ 23 ]. In 7xxx series alloys, the mismatch between η/η′ precipitates and the α-Al matrix triggers partial fragmentation or interfacial debonding of coarse MgZn₂ (η) precipitates, contributing to the refinement of precipitate morphology and a more refined distribution [ 24 ]. These micro-stress regions also create energetically favorable zones for the short-range rearrangement of solute atoms, enabling the denser formation of GP zones and a finer, more homogeneous distribution of η′ phases during the subsequent aging heat treatment [ 23 ,  24 – 25 ]. Accordingly, cryogenic treatment has been reported to accelerate precipitation kinetics and, together with increased dislocation density, yield modest yet measurable improvements in microhardness and wear resistance [ 26 ].

Additionally, low-temperature-induced contraction and micro-stress redistribution have been reported to reduce tensile residual stresses and promote locally compressive stress states in certain alloys, which can benefit surface integrity and machinability [ 27 ]. Consistent with these microstructural changes, machining of cryogenically treated materials has been associated with lower cutting forces, improved chip morphology, and enhanced surface integrity [ 28 ,  29 ]. However, since increased hardness after cryogenic treatment can generate higher contact pressure on the cutting tool, the optimization of cutting parameters is of critical importance [ 30 ]. Importantly, the response to cryogenic treatment is sensitive to the holding duration, which has been reported to modulate key microstructural features, including defect-structure evolution and residual-stress redistribution, as well as, in some studies, changes in precipitate characteristics and indications of grain refinement [ 22 ,  27 ,  31 ,  32 ,  33 – 34 ]. Therefore, a systematic investigation of the persistent effects of cryogenic holding time (CHT) on precipitate homogeneity, internal stress balance, and phase distribution is critical for the mechanical and machinability performance of AA7075 alloy [ 24 ,  35 ,  36 ].

Most studies on cryogenic treatment of AA7075 have primarily focused on mechanical properties or reported machinability using a limited set of outputs [ 37 ,  38 ]. For instance, Shen et al. [ 39 ] demonstrated that cryogenic treatment applied prior to milling significantly reduced machining-induced residual stresses and part deformation in aluminum alloys, and further ensured a more homogeneous distribution of stresses by lowering strain energy. In another study [ 40 ], cryogenic treatment was applied to the cutting tool during the milling of AA6061-T651 alloy, and its effects on surface roughness and tool wear were examined. Cryogenic technology is also widely investigated in the literature as an active cooling strategy to promote sustainable and eco-friendly manufacturing. In this context, Park et al. [ 41 ] demonstrated that cryogenic cooling serves as a viable green alternative by reducing cutting forces and tool wear compared to conventional flood cooling, highlighting its potential for energy consumption and sustainability. Similarly, Jain et al. [ 42 ] emphasized the use of liquid nitrogen as a sustainable ‘green coolant’ to overcome the health and environmental hazards of traditional metalworking fluids, noting significant improvements in chip morphology and thermal stability. However, studies that specifically evaluate the machinability of cryogenically pre-treated AA7075 remain scarce, and existing literature typically considers restricted performance indicators [ 43 ]. Consequently, a significant research gap exists regarding the systematic quantification of the persistent effects of CHT and its interaction with cutting parameters across coupled responses (force, temperature, vibration, power, and roughness), which this study aims to address.

sections.heading: Material and Cryogenic Treatment Procedure
paragraphs: Rolled AA7075-T6 aluminum alloy (supplied by SEYKOÇ Aluminum, Turkey) was used in this study. The nominal chemical composition is given in Table  1 .
Table 1 Nominal chemical composition of AA7075-T6 alloy (wt%) Element % Al % Zn % Cu % Cr % Ti % Fe % Mn % Zr % Ni % Other Al7075–T6 92.432 5.481 1.534 0.169 0.144 0.112 0.037 0.035 0.016 0.04

Prior to the milling experiments, four workpieces (80 mm × 100 mm × 20 mm) were prepared. Three workpieces were subjected to deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) at − 146 °C with holding times of 12, 24, and 36 h, respectively, while the remaining workpiece was kept in the as-received condition and used as the reference.

For microstructural characterization, both treated and untreated specimens were prepared by sequential grinding using SiC papers (P400, P800, P1200, and P2400), followed by polishing with 1 μm and 0.25 μm diamond suspensions. Final polishing was carried out using a 0.2 μm fumed silica suspension. The specimens were then ultrasonically cleaned in ethanol and air-dried prior to microscopy.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup
paragraphs: The experimental setup, including the CNC machine tool, cutting tool, dynamometer, accelerometer, infrared camera, and data acquisition systems, is schematically shown in Fig.  1 . Milling tests were performed on a HAAS VF-2 SS CNC vertical machining center. The workpiece material was AA7075, and all experiments were conducted under dry cutting conditions. An uncoated carbide end mill (WIDIN) with a 45° helix angle and three flutes was used as the cutting tool.

Vibration was monitored using a YMC 141A10 IEPE triaxial accelerometer, rigidly mounted on the dynamometer near the workpiece. Acceleration signals were sampled at 50 kHz using a YMC 9004 data-acquisition system and analyzed in the frequency domain, with the measurement axes aligned with the force-coordinate system.

Cutting temperature measurements were carried out using a FLIR T440 infrared (IR) thermal camera. During the measurements, the emissivity value specified in the manufacturer’s documentation was used, set to 0.04 [ 44 ]. All experiments were conducted under identical optical conditions. Thus, the measurements were intended to reflect relative temperature variations between different experimental conditions rather than absolute temperature values. Aluminum alloys are known to have low emissivity values that may vary depending on surface condition. To reduce measurement uncertainty associated with low emissivity and environmental reflections, the thermal camera was positioned approximately 650 mm (see Fig.  1 a, region 2) from the tool–workpiece contact zone with a direct view of the cutting region, without any protective machine enclosure in front of the camera. Maximum temperature values in the cutting zone were determined from the thermal images for each experiment and used in the comparative evaluations.

In addition, instantaneous power consumption was recorded from the CNC controller (spindle power/load output) during machining. Power data were evaluated together with force, vibration, and temperature to assess the energy response under different cutting conditions.

To ensure high experimental repeatability and consistency, all tests were conducted under identical conditions using the same tool geometry and cutting strategy. The workpiece dimensions and fixturing positions were kept constant throughout the experiments, and a new cutting tool was used for each run to avoid variability associated with tool wear. Data acquisition was performed using certified shielded cables routed away from power lines to minimize electromagnetic interference (EMI). In addition, a grounding protection scheme was applied to the vibration measurement system to reduce the influence of leakage currents (see Fig.  1 a, region 1). Pre-test noise analyses indicated that the signal-to-noise ratio was sufficient to ensure reliable signal interpretation, with only minor interference originating from unavoidable grid frequencies and inherent system dynamics. Importantly, these noise characteristics remained consistent across all 108 experimental runs (comprising 36 unique parameter combinations with three replicates each), preserving the validity of comparative analyses. Therefore, the acquired force and vibration signals were evaluated in their raw form without additional filtering, ensuring that the results accurately reflect the physical behavior of the process.

Fig. 1 a  Annotated photograph of the experimental setup: (1) dynamometer, workpiece, accelerometer, and grounding connection; (2) measured distance between the thermal camera and the cutting tool;  b  schematic illustration of the experimental setup

sections.heading: Control Factors and Design of Experiments
paragraphs: In total, 36 unique parameter combinations (3 × 3 × 4) were tested. To ensure repeatability, all trials were conducted under the same tool, fixturing, and dry-cutting conditions, following an identical toolpath strategy. Measurements of cutting force, vibration, temperature, and surface roughness were taken according to a predefined and consistent measurement protocol. Each condition was repeated three times, and the mean values were used for subsequent analysis.

sections.heading: Mechanical and Microstructural Characterization
paragraphs: Hardness was evaluated for both cryogenically treated and untreated specimens using Brinell macrohardness testing (HBW 2.5/62.5) in accordance with ASTM E10. A 2.5 mm hardened steel ball and a load of 62.5 kgf were applied, and at least five indents were made at different locations on each specimen; the arithmetic mean and standard deviation were reported.

The microstructural properties and surface morphologies of the specimens were examined using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) (Hitachi SU8700). Analyses were performed under an accelerating voltage of 10 kV and a working distance of 12.3 mm. The surfaces of the treated and untreated specimens were evaluated comparatively. Additionally, Energy-Dispersive X-Ray Spectroscopy (EDS) was performed to determine the surface elemental composition.

The phase composition, crystal structure, and changes in lattice parameters of the specimens were investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD). XRD analyses were carried out using a Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer. Measurements employed Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 Å) with a scanning range of 20°–80° (2θ). The scans were performed in the Bragg–Brentano (θ–2θ) geometry with a step size of 0.02°. The obtained diffractograms were compared to assess variations in phase and crystal structure as a function of CHT.

sections.heading: Entropy-based Grey Relational Analysis for Multi-objective Optimization
paragraphs: The Entropy-weighted GRA method was employed to comprehensively evaluate multiple performance criteria, specifically cutting force, vibration, temperature, power consumption, and surface roughness, that possess distinct units and scales. GRA is a widely utilized and effective technique in multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) problems for determining the proximity of alternatives to the ideal solution.

sections.heading: Data Normalization

paragraphs: Conventional GRA typically assumes equal weights for all criteria. However, in practice, the information contributed by each criterion varies significantly. In this study, the Entropy method was utilized to calculate weights based on the information content of each criterion, which were subsequently integrated into the GRA framework. Entropy weighting assigns higher importance to criteria with greater variability, reflecting their higher information content.

sections.heading: Microstructural and Phase Analysis Results
paragraphs: The BSE image of the AA7075-T6 specimen subjected to cryogenic treatment (36 h) reveals secondary phase regions aligned along the extrusion direction, distinguished by their bright contrast within the matrix (Fig.  3 a). These bright regions correspond to clusters of intermetallic phases containing elements with higher atomic numbers. Point EDS analyses obtained from the locations marked as Spectrum 1 (Speck 1) and Spectrum 2 (Speck 2) in Fig.  3 a support the compositional character of these phases.

The EDS elemental mapping images in Fig.  4 b confirm the presence of both Cu-rich and Mg/Zn-rich secondary phases in areas where Mg–Zn–Cu elements are co-enriched. Speck 1 exhibits a high Al content (≈ 87.9 wt%) and low alloying element ratios, indicating that this region represents the α-Al matrix. In contrast, Speck 2 shows an increase in Fe content together with a decrease in the Al ratio, suggesting that this region corresponds to an Fe-containing complex intermetallic phase. At Speck 3, the high Cu content (≈ 45.2 wt%), lower Al ratio (≈ 26.2 wt%), and co-enriched Zn–Mg elements indicate the presence of Cu-rich intermetallic phases (e.g., Al₂Cu and/or Al₂CuMg) (Fig.  3 c).

Fig. 3 a  BSE (Backscattered Electron) image of the cryogenically treated (36 h) AA7075-T6 alloy. Intermetallic particles appearing in white/grey tones within the matrix and extending parallel to the extrusion direction are evident. The regions where EDS point analyses were conducted are marked as Spectrum 1, Spectrum 2, and Spectrum 3.  b  EDS distribution (mapping) maps of Al, Mg, Fe, and Cu elements belonging to the region indicated by the white box in ( a ). The maps show intermetallic phase clusters in regions where Mg and Cu elements are locally enriched. ( c ) Normalized EDS point analyses (wt%) obtained from points Spectrum 1, Spectrum 2, and Spectrum 3 numbered in ( a ). While Spectrum 1 stands out with high Al content characteristic of the matrix, Spectrum 2 corresponds to an Fe-containing complex intermetallic structure, and Spectrum 3 corresponds to a distinctly Cu-rich intermetallic phase

The XRD patterns of the AA7075 alloy before cryogenic treatment and after 36 h of cryogenic holding are shown separately in Fig.  4 a to avoid graphical overlap. The diffraction patterns of both specimens contain characteristic reflections corresponding to the face-centered cubic (FCC) aluminum phase, with main peaks located at approximately 38°, 45°, 65°, and 78° corresponding to the (111), (200), (220), and (311) planes, respectively. Prior to cryogenic treatment, no distinct second-phase peak structure was observed; however, trace reflections attributed to the MgZn₂ (η) phase could be very weakly distinguished in the spectrum [ 45 ]. After cryogenic treatment, these low-intensity reflections corresponding to the MgZn₂ phase appeared slightly more pronounced.

Fig. 4 a  XRD patterns of the AA7075 alloy in the as-received condition and after cryogenic treatment. Both patterns exhibit the characteristic FCC Al reflections at approximately 38° (111), 45° (200), 65° (220), and 78° (311). Weak η-MgZn₂ reflections (e.g., near 37.3° and 78.48°) become slightly more distinguishable after cryogenic treatment, while no new phases are detected.  b  Variation of hardness as a function of CHT, showing a progressive increase in hardness with increasing holding duration; error bars represent the standard deviation

sections.heading: Hardness Variation with CHT
paragraphs: Brinell hardness measurements were performed on untreated specimens and those subjected to cryogenic treatment for 12, 24, and 36 h, respectively. For each specimen, five distinct measurements were taken from different regions, and the mean hardness value is presented in Fig.  4 b along with its standard deviation.

The results indicate a gradual increase in Brinell hardness with increasing CHT. The mean hardness was 173.6 HB for the untreated specimen and increased to 175.4 HB, 177.2 HB, and 179.6 HB after 12, 24, and 36 h of cryogenic treatment, respectively. A one-way ANOVA ( n  = 5) showed that the effect of CHT on hardness was statistically significant (F(3,16) = 9.31,  p  < 0.01), although the magnitude of the increase was limited.

sections.heading: Vibration Response (PSD-Based Metrics)
paragraphs: During milling operations, acceleration signals in the X, Y, and Z directions were recorded for each experimental condition using a triaxial accelerometer, and the total Power Spectral Density (PSD) was calculated from these acceleration data. The obtained vibration accelerations and total PSD results are presented in Table  7 . The highest total PSD value was recorded in Experiment 30. Additionally, the X-axis emerged as the dominant vibration component in the majority of the experiments. However, under certain conditions, elevated vibration components were observed in different axes (e.g., 4.503 g²/Hz in the Z-axis for Experiment 27, and 3.157 g²/Hz in the Y-axis for Experiment 23). Conversely, total PSD values remained lower in Experiments 7, 34, 35, and 31.

A comparison of PSD distributions and frequency intensities for all experiments is provided in Fig.  9 . In the PSD plot for the X-axis (Fig.  9 a), a high-energy region was identified in the 0–3 kHz range. While energy levels decreased in the 3–8 kHz band, regions sensitive to experimental parameters were evident around 6–7 kHz and in the 14–16 kHz range. Energy concentration was detected across all axes at approximately 24 kHz. In the Y-axis plot, lower energy levels were observed compared to other axes, particularly around 15–16 kHz. The Z-axis exhibited a general behavior similar to that of the X-axis.
Fig. 9 PSD plots for all experiments: ( a ) for X-axis, ( b ) for Y-axis, and ( c ) for Z-axis

In Fig.  10 , the vibration responses of the tool under cutting load and no-load conditions are compared based on the Power Spectral Density (PSD) of triaxial (X, Y, Z) acceleration data from Experiment 31. In the low-frequency band (approximately 0–4 kHz) indicated by 1, 2, and 3 in the figure, harmonics with significantly increased amplitudes under load are observed. This increase is particularly higher for the X-axis (Fig.  10 a) compared to the other axes. However, when the amplitude variation in this region is compared with that in Fig.  9 , it is evident that it exhibits a similar trend across all experiments and is independent of the cutting parameters.

In contrast, it was determined that the harmonics around 12 kHz and 24 kHz, marked with number 4, appeared with similar amplitudes under both load and no-load conditions and were unaffected by cutting forces. The frequency range of approximately 14–16 kHz, indicated by 5 in Fig.  10 a and c, contains harmonics whose amplitudes increase significantly during cutting and, compared with Fig.  9 , demonstrate sensitivity to cutting parameters. No variation was observed in this frequency band for the Y-axis (Fig.  10 b).
Fig. 10 PSD plots of vibrations measured while the tool is under chip load and under no-load conditions: ( a ) for X-axis, ( b ) for Y-axis, and ( c ) for Z-axis

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: This study investigates how cryogenic holding time (CHT) and cutting parameters influence the milling performance of AA7075-T6. Beyond statistical evaluation (ANOVA and Entropy-GRA), the observed trends are interpreted based on underlying microstructural evolution and thermomechanical mechanisms.

sections.heading: Microstructural Evolution Induced by Cryogenic Treatment
paragraphs: A collective evaluation of the obtained BSE, EDS, and XRD findings regarding the effects of cryogenic treatment on the microstructural properties of AA7075 alloy indicates that no fundamental change occurred in the phase structure; however, distinct stress-induced microstructural rearrangements took place within the matrix (Figs.  3  and  4 ). BSE images revealed that Cu-, Mg-, and Zn-rich intermetallic phases aligned along the extrusion direction persisted after cryogenic treatment and preserved their morphological integrity (Fig.  3 a). Nevertheless, due to the spatial resolution of BSE and the detection limits of EDS, the direct resolution of minute changes that might occur in the fine precipitate population is limited with these techniques.

In XRD analyses, trace reflections belonging to the α(Al) matrix phase and MgZn₂ (η) precipitates were detected in both pre- and post-treatment specimens (Fig.  4 ). The shift of the main diffraction peaks towards higher 2θ values after cryogenic treatment suggests a limited reduction in the matrix lattice parameters. This shift is attributed to microstress fields resulting from the differences in thermal expansion coefficients between the matrix and intermetallic phases during cooling, rather than a phase transformation [ 37 ]. Although some researchers [ 22 ,  38 ,  47 ] have suggested that coarse secondary phases partially dissolve into the matrix during cryogenic treatment, this interpretation remains debatable due to the extremely limited diffusion coefficients at such low temperatures [ 43 ]. The findings obtained in the present study do not support the hypothesis of phase dissolution; instead, they indicate that the observed variations can be better explained by microstructural rearrangements caused by internal stress fields arising from thermal contraction differences and the accompanying limited increase in dislocation density [ 48 ,  49 ].

The limited increase of hardness measured after cryogenic treatment is attributed to these stress-induced microstructural rearrangements within the matrix [ 45 ]. The modest nature of this increase is consistent with the restricted diffusion at low temperatures and the absence of a distinct change in precipitate morphology on a macro scale. In future studies, quantitative analysis of microstrain (e.g., peak broadening analysis, Williamson-Hall/Rietveld methods) and evaluation of the precipitate structure via TEM would contribute to a more precise interpretation of the microstructural mechanisms of cryogenic treatment.

sections.heading: Influence of Machining Parameters on Performance Criteria
Effect of Feed Rate on Cutting Force Mechanisms
paragraphs: Upon examining the data in Fig.  6 , a clear increase rise in cutting forces with increasing feed rate is evident. This observed increasing trend can be attributed to the augmented unit chip load and the consequently elevated resistance to plastic deformation. Consequently, the results of this study confirm the determinant role of the feed parameter in cutting dynamics and align with the general consensus in the literature.

sections.heading: Dominant Parameters Affecting Cutting Temperature
paragraphs: As shown in Fig.  7 , the highest values of temperature, force, and vibration were recorded in untreated specimens (CHT = 0 h); conversely, a distinct improvement in machinability was observed with the extended CHT. Thermal analysis findings reveal that while cutting temperatures generally tended to decrease with increasing CHT, this reduction exhibited a non-linear and fluctuating distribution. Theoretically, the increase in hardness expected with cryogenic treatment [ 56 ,  57 – 58 ] would raise the energy required for plastic deformation in the primary shear zone, thereby increasing the temperature. However, the potential of cryogenic treatment to alter the material's thermal conductivity may counterbalance this effect by influencing the rate of heat evacuation through the chips. Consequently, the influence of CHT on temperature can be largely attributed to the mechanism of heat evacuation via chips.

On the other hand, the non-linear trend observed in temperature variation is attributed to process stability. Inappropriate selection of cutting parameter combinations may disrupt the deformation mechanism, leading to increases in cutting forces, friction, chip flow resistance, and vibrations. This state of instability can trigger sudden temperature spikes in the cutting zone, contradicting the expected cooling trend.

sections.heading: Correlation Between Microstructural Rearrangements and Machining Mechanics
paragraphs: Furthermore, cryogenic treatment promotes microstructural homogeneity, reducing tool-chip contact length and friction. The resulting reduction in friction lowers heat generation in the secondary deformation zone while stabilizing chip formation. Consequently, improved flow dynamics accelerate heat removal via the chips, preventing thermal accumulation at the tool-workpiece interface.
Fig. 15 Theoretical model of heat generation and distribution in the metal cutting process (three-zone orthogonal cutting)

Regarding dynamic stability, the limited 4% contribution of CHT to vibration (PSD) indicates that the vibration response is governed primarily by cutting speed (40%) and feed rate (30%). Therefore, the effect of CHT should be interpreted as secondary under the present experimental conditions. This limited contribution may be related to subtle changes in the material response after cryogenic treatment, such as variations in deformation stability and frictional behavior during cutting. However, because cutting speed, feed rate, and CHT were varied simultaneously in the present full factorial design, the direct effect of CHT on vibration mechanisms could not be isolated reliably. Further studies under constant cutting parameters are therefore needed to clarify this relationship in more detail.

sections.heading: Cutting Parameters and CHT
paragraphs: Although CHT significantly influenced cutting temperature and cutting force, the results indicate that vibration, surface roughness, and power consumption were predominantly governed by cutting parameters, particularly feed per tooth. This suggests that while cryogenic treatment modifies the intrinsic material response, the dynamic behavior of the machining process remains strongly dependent on process parameters.

The dominant influence of feed rate on surface roughness and vibration can be explained by its direct control over chip thickness and tool–workpiece interaction. Higher feed rates increase mechanical loading and surface irregularities, leading to higher vibration amplitudes and degraded surface quality. These findings are in agreement with established machining theory and previous experimental studies.

sections.heading: Multi-Response Interpretation of Optimal Machining Condition
paragraphs: The multi-criteria optimization results further highlight the importance of considering coupled performance responses rather than single-output evaluation. The optimal condition identified through Entropy-weighted GRA represents a balanced trade-off between thermal, mechanical, and dynamic responses.

Notably, while power consumption slightly increased under optimal conditions, significant reductions in cutting force, temperature, and vibration indicate an overall improvement in process stability and machining efficiency. This confirms that minimizing all responses simultaneously may not be feasible, and that optimization should focus on achieving a balanced, stable machining regime.

sections.heading: Dynamic Response Characteristics under Cutting Forces
paragraphs: The vibration analyses conducted clearly demonstrate the impact of cutting forces on the dynamic behavior of the system during the milling process. In particular, the distinct increase in the amplitudes of high-energy harmonics observed across all axes within the 0–4 kHz frequency range under cutting load indicates that these components are directly excited by periodic cutting forces. The independent manifestation of these harmonics, regardless of cutting parameters, suggests that the system exhibits an inherent response to forced excitation within this frequency band.

Conversely, the presence of harmonics in the approximate 14–16 kHz band, which exhibit amplitude growth solely under load and demonstrate sensitivity to varying cutting parameters, reveals that this region possesses dynamic characteristics responsive to machining conditions. This phenomenon is critical for process monitoring and control, suggesting that optimal machining parameters can be utilized to mitigate vibration levels in this specific frequency region. Furthermore, the harmonics around 12 kHz and 24 kHz, which maintained similar amplitudes under both load and no-load conditions, are thought to be associated with the system’s structural natural frequencies or background components originating from the measurement system [ 88 ]. These findings demonstrate that vibration responses generated during milling are shaped not only by the loading effect but also by the structural characteristics of the system, thereby underscoring the necessity of a multi-dimensional analysis approach.

sections.heading: Comparison with the Literature
paragraphs: Cryogenic treatment, particularly Deep Cryogenic Treatment (DCT), is among the prominent methods that significantly influence the machining/forming processes and the microstructure–property–performance relationship. In this context, two main axes emerge in the literature: (i) machinability/surface integrity (surface roughness, tool wear, cutting temperature/tribology) [ 43 ,  89 ], and (ii) mechanical properties/deformability (yield-tensile strength, hardness, forming behavior performance). Notably, investigations into the machinability of aluminum alloys subjected to cryogenic treatment (specifically DCT) remain quite limited.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Future work should include the quantification of microstrain and precipitation features (e.g., via Williamson–Hall/Rietveld analysis and TEM), and the extension of the optimization framework to include tool wear and surface integrity metrics (e.g., residual stress and microhardness gradients) to further strengthen industrial relevance.
